idea.why: Clean three-phase decomposition with one specialist per source and a composer that owns presentation only. The division is real, not cosmetic: the triage and calendar prompts are forbidden from writing the briefing, and the composer from inventing facts, so each concern lives in exactly one place. Minor ding: the agents carry no tools, so the crew is really three sequenced prompts.

structure.why: Mostly purpose-built types with no Code node reinventing any of it. The weak point is using the agent node three times for what are one-shot toolless summarisation calls; a chain is the node meant for that, and the tool-calling loop is unused. Twelve nodes is proportionate and the sticky notes carry real handover instructions rather than decoration.

connections.why: The wiring matches the actual dependencies: the calendar lane waits only on the trigger, so the two independent fetches genuinely fan out instead of being serialised, then rejoin at a Merge where they truly converge. Small wart: the merged output is never read, so it functions purely as a join gate.

answer.why: End to end this does what was asked and a reader would recognise their request. Two gaps: dashboard is answered as an emailed page rather than anything you can revisit, and the composer's fragment contract is enforced by prose alone, so a chatty model returning a code fence would land raw text inside the shell.

appraisal: The shape a competent user would reach for: one schedule fanning into two independent fetches, each aggregated so its specialist fires once, both rejoining at a Merge before a composer that owns nothing but presentation. The prompts are unusually disciplined about role boundaries and about not inventing senders or times, and the template gives the briefing a real visual hierarchy instead of dumping markdown into an email. What it gets wrong is small but real: three agent nodes with no tools are doing chain work, the Merge output is discarded in favour of node references, and the briefing exists only as one outbound email. The first change is swapping those toolless agents for chains, or giving them actual tools so the multi-agent framing earns itself.
